title: Mathematical Setting: Euler Product and Riemann Zeta at s=2
content:
The module docstring states the core identity ∏_p (1-p⁻²)⁻¹ = π²/6 and identifies the two Mathlib theorems that make it a two-line proof: `riemannZeta_eulerProduct_tprod` (Euler product for ζ(s)) and `riemannZeta_two` (ζ(2) = π²/6). The references cite Euler's 1737 paper 'Variae observationes circa series infinitas', the first appearance of the product formula.

This entry is one of a sibling family: `basel-problem` proves the sum ∑ 1/n² = π²/6, `geometric-series-oq-03` derives the Euler product via geometric series, and this entry (`oq-04`) combines them at s=2. Together they cover Euler's complete 1737 argument.

The proof is stated over ℂ (not ℝ) because Mathlib's `riemannZeta` function is defined as a meromorphic function on all of ℂ, and the Euler product theorem is proved in that generality. The specialization to s=2 is then a corollary. This generality connects this entry to the Riemann hypothesis: ζ(s) has non-trivial zeros only for 0 < Re(s) < 1 (conjectured to all lie on Re(s) = 1/2), and the Euler product ∏_p (1-p⁻ˢ)⁻¹ = ζ(s) holds only for Re(s) > 1 (where ζ(s) ≠ 0). The zeros of ζ(s) are exactly where the product formula breaks down.
mathContext: The Riemann zeta function: $\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-s}$ for $\text{Re}(s) > 1$, extended meromorphically to $\mathbb{C} \setminus \{1\}$. Euler product: $\zeta(s) = \prod_p (1-p^{-s})^{-1}$ for $\text{Re}(s) > 1$ (absolute convergence region). At $s = 2$: $\zeta(2) = \pi^2/6$ (Basel). The Riemann Hypothesis asserts the non-trivial zeros of $\zeta(s)$ all satisfy $\text{Re}(s) = 1/2$. Mathlib: `riemannZeta : ℂ → ℂ` (module `Mathlib.NumberTheory.ZetaFunctions.RiemannZeta`).

title: Imports and the Re(2) > 1 Helper Lemma
content: The file imports three targeted Mathlib modules: DirichletLSeries (for the Euler product theorem), HurwitzZetaValues (for ζ(2) = π²/6), and ZetaValues (for the Basel sum). The helper `two_re_gt_one` establishes Re(2) > 1, which is the convergence hypothesis for Euler product theorems in Mathlib. This trivial lemma is needed because Mathlib's Euler product theorems are stated over ℂ with a general Re(s) > 1 hypothesis.
mathContext: Mathlib's `riemannZeta_eulerProduct_tprod` has type: `∀ (s : ℂ), 1 < s.re → ∏' p : Nat.Primes, (1 - (p : ℂ)^(-s))⁻¹ = riemannZeta s`. This holds for all $s$ with $\text{Re}(s) > 1$, corresponding to absolute convergence of the Dirichlet series $\zeta(s) = \sum n^{-s}$. At $s=2$: $\text{Re}(2) = 2 > 1$, so the convergence condition is satisfied and the product equals $\zeta(2) = \pi^2/6$.

title: Tprod Form: The Infinite Product as a Value
content: The `euler_product_pi_sq_div_six` theorem states the product as an equality of complex numbers: ∏' p (1 - p^{-2})^{-1} = π²/6. The proof is exactly two rewrites: first `rw [← riemannZeta_two]` replaces π²/6 with ζ(2), then `exact riemannZeta_eulerProduct_tprod two_re_gt_one` applies the Euler product theorem. This two-line proof illustrates how formal mathematics can capture deep results by combining library theorems.
mathContext: The `∏'` (tprod, topological product) in Lean is the unconditional product of a family indexed by `Nat.Primes`. For Dirichlet series, the Euler product $\prod_p (1-p^{-s})^{-1} = \zeta(s)$ holds for $\text{Re}(s) > 1$ and can be interpreted as: (1) a value identity (tprod form), (2) a convergence statement (HasProd), or (3) a limit of finite products (Tendsto). Each captures a different aspect of the same mathematical truth.

title: HasProd Form: Explicit Convergence Certificate
content: The `euler_product_hasProd` theorem states the same result as a `HasProd` proposition, which in Mathlib/topology means: the product of the given family converges to π²/6 in the topological sense. This is stronger than a plain equality — it asserts the product converges (not just 'if it converges, its value is...'). The proof is identical in structure to the tprod form, using `riemannZeta_eulerProduct_hasProd`.
mathContext: `HasProd f a` means the net of finite partial products converges to $a$ in the topology. For $f_p = (1 - p^{-2})^{-1}$ over primes: $\text{HasProd}\, f\, (\pi^2/6)$ certifies both convergence and the limiting value. The HasProd formulation is often preferred in Mathlib for products because it bundles the convergence proof. The three formulations (tprod, HasProd, Tendsto) are equivalent for absolutely convergent products.

title: Tendsto Form: Finite Products Over Primes Converging to π²/6
content: The `euler_product_tendsto` theorem gives the most computationally intuitive form: the sequence of finite products ∏_{p < n} (1-p^{-2})^{-1} converges to π²/6 as n → ∞. This is what Euler would have computed numerically. The `Nat.primesBelow n` function returns the primes below n as a Finset, making the finite product computable. This form connects abstract infinite products to approximation sequences.
mathContext: The tendsto form: $\lim_{n\to\infty} \prod_{p < n, p\text{ prime}} (1-p^{-2})^{-1} = \pi^2/6$. For example: $\prod_{p \le 7} (1-p^{-2})^{-1} = \frac{4}{3}\cdot\frac{9}{8}\cdot\frac{25}{24}\cdot\frac{49}{48} = \frac{8820}{6720} \approx 1.3125$, while $\pi^2/6 \approx 1.6449$. The convergence is slow because of the prime number theorem: adding prime $p$ multiplies by $(1-p^{-2})^{-1} \approx 1 + p^{-2}$, contributing $\sim 1/p^2$ at each step.

title: The Basel Sum and Euler's Original Argument
content: The `basel_sum` theorem restates the Basel result from Mathlib as a `HasSum`: ∑ 1/n² = π²/6. It is a one-liner pointing to Mathlib's `hasSum_zeta_two`. The historical context comment below explains Euler's 1737 product argument: expanding each (1-p^{-s})^{-1} as a geometric series and using unique factorization to identify the product with the Dirichlet series. The identity ∏_p (1-1/p²) = 6/π² ≈ 0.6079 equals the probability that two random integers are coprime (Cesàro 1881).
mathContext: The Basel sum: $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6}$ (Euler 1734). The Euler product: $\zeta(s) = \prod_p (1-p^{-s})^{-1}$ for $\text{Re}(s) > 1$ (Euler 1737). At $s=2$: $\sum \frac{1}{n^2} = \prod_p \frac{1}{1-p^{-2}} = \frac{\pi^2}{6}$. The coprimality probability: $\Pr[\gcd(m,n)=1] = \prod_p (1-p^{-2}) = \frac{6}{\pi^2} \approx 60.79\%$. Euler's argument used unique factorization: $\prod_p \sum_{k=0}^\infty p^{-ks} = \sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-s}$.
